transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me, Doctor. I really appreciate you taking the time. I'm... I'm hoping I'm in the right place. It's just that, lately, the thought of getting on an airplane... it just really scares me. I know it probably sounds silly, and I know it doesn't make any sense, but my body just tells me that the plane is going to fall. Is that... is that something you can help with? I hope it's not too trivial.
Is it just airplanes that scare you, or are there other situations that make you feel anxious or fearful?

Um, no, it's... it's really just airplanes, I think. I don't want you to think I'm just a nervous person in general, because I'm actually very calm most of the time. I handle stress and everyday things just fine. It's literally just this one specific thing... being up in the air in a plane. 

Is that... does that make sense to you, Doctor? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of information. I just wouldn't want you to get the wrong impression of me.
How long have you been experiencing this fear of airplanes?

Well, it hasn't been my whole life, I promise. I don't want you to think I've always been irrational about this. It's really only been about... I'd say seven months? Give or take? 

Um... I took a flight on a small plane back then, and it was just terribly turbulent. Really, really rough. And, well... to be completely honest, I'm a little embarrassed to even bring it up, because it's not my proudest moment, but that flight happened right after I... I lost my job at the clinic. So maybe I was already a bit on edge when I got on board? I don't know. 

Does that timeline make sense to you, Doctor? I hope that's the kind of detail you're looking for. I just want to make sure I'm being helpful.
Has your fear of airplanes stopped you from doing things you want or need to do?

Well, I... I really try not to let it affect my responsibilities, because I know how important my work is. But, um... if I'm being completely honest, and I hope you won't judge me too harshly for this, it has gotten in the way a bit. 

I've had to, um, cancel some of my clinic coverage, which I feel terrible about. And I've skipped a few important medical meetings... and even put off visiting my family back in Honduras. It's just... I can't even get myself to go to the airport unless I'm absolutely terrified, shaking, and literally having to hold on to someone the entire time. It's so embarrassing for a grown man, especially a physician, to act like that. 

I really try to push through it, I do. Does that... does that answer your question, Doctor? I just hope you don't think less of me for letting it get to this point.
Have you experienced anxiety in any other specific situations besides flying?

Um, no, no other situations. Like I said before, it's really just the airplanes. I... I hope I'm being clear about that. I don't want you to think I'm just an anxious person in general, because I'm really not. I handle the clinic, my patients, everything else just fine. It's just... flying. 

I'm sorry if I'm repeating myself, Doctor. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture. Is that... is that helpful?
Have you been experiencing any general feelings of anxiety or apprehension that are not related to flying?

No, no, nothing like that. I really don't want you to get the wrong idea about me. I'm usually very put together, you know? I manage a lot of stress at the clinic without any problems. 

It's... it's honestly just the planes. I don't sit around worrying about other things or feeling on edge during the day. I sleep fine, I work fine... it's just this one silly thing that I can't seem to shake. 

I hope that makes sense? I just really want to reassure you that I'm not, you know, falling apart everywhere else. I'm doing my best to keep everything else running smoothly. Is that... does that sound okay to you?
Have you been avoiding thoughts or conversations about airplanes in addition to avoiding the act of flying itself?

Oh, no, um... I don't avoid talking about them at all. If my colleagues are discussing their vacations or, you know, if I see a plane on the news, it doesn't bother me. I can think about them perfectly fine. It's really just... just the actual flying part. 

I'd never want to make anyone else feel awkward if they want to talk about their travel plans, so I just listen and converse like normal. I hope that shows I'm not completely, um, irrational about everything? I really do try to keep this whole issue contained so it doesn't bother anyone else. 

I can definitely talk about them with you as much as you need. Is that... is that the kind of detail you were looking for? I want to make sure I'm answering your questions properly.
Do you experience any physical symptoms, such as a racing heart or sweating, when you think about getting on an airplane?

Well, um... I guess I do, a little bit. It's... it's honestly a bit embarrassing to admit. I don't want to sound dramatic or anything, especially being a doctor myself, you know? I feel like I should be able to control it better. 

But, yes, if I even just get an email at work about covering a rural shift that would require taking a flight... my heart just starts pounding right away. My hands get all sweaty, and, um... I actually feel like I can't breathe until I just click away and close the message. 

I know it's silly, and I always make sure nobody at the clinic sees me acting like that. I just quietly close the email and try to compose myself so I don't bother anyone else. Does that... is that the kind of physical reaction you were asking about? I really hope I'm giving you the right information.
Have you ever had a panic attack while on an airplane?

No, no, I've never actually had a full-blown panic attack on a plane. I mean, I've always managed to avoid getting on one since this whole thing started, so... I haven't really put myself in that situation. 

I really try to be responsible about it, you know? I know my limits, and I just make sure I don't put myself in a position where I might lose control or, um, cause a scene that would inconvenience the flight crew or the other passengers. I would feel just awful if I ruined someone else's trip because I couldn't keep it together. 

So, no, no panic attacks on planes. I just stay on the ground and keep things manageable. Is that... I hope that's a good thing, right? That I haven't let it get to that point?
Have you been avoiding places or activities that remind you of airplanes?

Well, um... I guess I do avoid the airport itself. I really try not to let it affect my responsibilities, but... well, I have had to cancel some rural clinic coverage, and, um, I've skipped a few medical conferences that were out of state. 

I know it's not ideal, and I feel terrible letting my colleagues down. I even... I've even put off visiting my family in Honduras. I just... I can't make myself go to the airport. The only way I could even imagine getting through the terminal is if I was shaking and physically holding onto someone the entire time, and I... I couldn't do that to anyone. I wouldn't want to be such a burden or make a spectacle of myself. 

So, I just avoid going altogether. I hope you don't think less of me for that... I really do try to handle it as best I can without inconveniencing people. Is that... does that answer your question?
Was there something specific about the turbulent flight seven months ago that triggered your fear of airplanes?

Well, um... I guess it was just the whole experience. It's... it's a bit hard to talk about, honestly, because I feel like I should have been able to handle it better. But, um, it was about seven months ago, right after I lost my position at the clinic. 

I was already feeling really low and stressed, and then I took this flight on a small plane, and... the turbulence was just awful. It felt like we were dropping out of the sky. I know turbulence is normal, and as a doctor, I know the statistics on flight safety, so I really shouldn't have reacted the way I did. I tried so hard to stay calm so I wouldn't worry the other passengers, but... ever since then, for the last seven months, I just can't shake this feeling. 

I hope I'm not making too big a deal out of it. I know people go through much worse, and I really want to move past this so I can be more reliable for my colleagues and my family. Does that make sense? Is it normal for something like that to trigger this kind of reaction for so long?
Are there any other areas of your daily life, besides traveling, where this fear of airplanes is affecting your decisions or actions?

Well, um... I guess it mostly just comes back to the traveling part, but... it does kind of ripple out into other things. I mean, I really try not to let it show, but... well, because I've had to turn down that rural clinic coverage that requires a flight, it's... it's actually cost me some income. And, um, I worry—well, I know—that some of my colleagues are starting to question if they can really rely on me. 

I've always prided myself on being dependable, so that's been really hard to swallow. And like I mentioned before, I've missed those important medical conferences, which isn't great for keeping up with things, and... and I've delayed seeing my family in Honduras. 

I know it probably sounds like I'm letting this control my life, and I really, really don't want to be that kind of person. I'm trying to figure out how to fix it so I can be a good doctor and a good son again. I hope you can understand that I'm doing my best... does it seem like I'm at least trying to handle it the right way?
Are there any situations or activities related to airplanes that you avoid thinking about or participating in, aside from actually flying?

Well, um... I guess... I mean, I really try to keep my thoughts positive, you know? I don't want to dwell on it. But... well, if I'm being completely honest, it does affect me even when I'm not near an airport. 

Like... um, sometimes I'll just get an email at work. Just a normal email asking if someone can cover a rural shift that requires taking a small plane. And... I know it's silly, I know I'm perfectly safe sitting at my desk, but... my heart just starts pounding right away. My hands get all sweaty, and I feel like I just can't catch my breath. It's... it's embarrassing, really. I have to just close the message immediately to make it stop. 

I know a doctor shouldn't react that way to an email. I really try to hide it so no one at the clinic notices. I hope you don't think I'm completely falling apart... I mean, it's just a physical reaction, right? Is it okay that I just close the email to handle it? I just don't want to make a scene at work.
Are there other aspects of your daily routine or personal relationships that are being affected by your fear of airplanes?

Well, um... no, I don't think so. I mean, I really try to keep it contained, you know? Like I mentioned, it's mostly just the... the rural coverage and delaying the trip to see my parents. 

But my day-to-day routine here, like driving to the clinic, seeing my local patients, or just spending time with friends... I make sure it doesn't get in the way of any of that. I really don't want to be a burden to anyone, so I work hard to keep everything else as normal as possible. I don't want people to think I'm incapable. 

So, aside from the flying part, I think I'm managing the rest of my life pretty well. At least, I hope I am... does it seem to you like I'm keeping it together everywhere else? I really am trying my best to not let it spill over.
